results.title: A Generalized Difference-in-Differences Estimator for Randomized Stepped-Wedge and Observational Staggered Adoption Settings
results.content: Across settings, the analysis of the data generated from staggered treatment adoption requires careful consideration of the desired estimand, assumptions about the treatment effect, consideration of heterogeneity across units, time periods, and treatment regimens, and appropriate consideration of variance and correlation. In the observational staggered adoption setting, approaches to address the biases that can arise in two-way fixed-effects models (see, e.g., Goodman-Bacon (2021) and Imai & Kim (2021)) have included adjusting the interpretation based on the identifying assumptions as in Athey & Imbens (2022), specifying “dynamic” (time-varying) treatment effects as in Sun & Abraham (2021), and isolating, excluding, or weighting effect estimators targeting specific group-time effects as in Callaway & Sant’Anna (2021) and de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille (2020). This paper introduces a generalized estimator framework that can target a variety of estimands specified by investigators under different sets of assumptions about treatment effect homogeneity. The framework has the advantages of: (1) unifying methods across different settings, assumptions, and target estimands; (2) minimizing variance under certain variance-specific assumptions while preserving validity; (3) easing interpretability and improving robustness by explicitly identifying weights on the two-by-two DID estimators and on the observations themselves; and (4) permitting sensitivity analysis across heterogeneity and variance assumptions. results.title: Guide for comparing estimators of policy change effects on health - PMC
results.content: Around 2020, new estimators were proposed mostly in the econometric literature (with one article in the epidemiologic literature) to estimate the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) for difference in differences (DID) settings where polices are introduced at different times across treated units. The two-way fixed effect estimator, which had previously been the standard approach for these settings, was shown to be biased and/or to estimate an unintuitive target parameter when treatment effects were dynamic or heterogeneous (when effects differed over time or across adoption cohorts, respectively) (1). Newly introduced estimators that addressed the limitations of the two-way fixed effects estimator include the Group-Time ATT estimator introduced by Callaway and Sant’Anna (2), the Cohort ATT estimator introduced by Sun and Abraham (3), and the Target Trial estimator developed for this context by Ben-Michael, Feller, and Stuart (4). For example, heterogeneity of the treatment’s effect across adoption cohorts (characteristic #3) changes the parameter being estimated because the two-way fixed effects estimate is a weighted average of all ATTs, where the weights are a function of both the number of units treated at each time and the treatment variance, which is influenced by the time of policy adoption during the study period (characteristic #1) (1). This is an important aspect of the new literature, as it shows how the two-way fixed effects estimate can be affected by the timing of policy introductions in terms of the total length of the panel analyzed by the researcher (4). A researcher can obtain a different two-way fixed effects estimate of the policy’s effect on the outcome solely by adding more pre-policy time (or post-policy time) to the analysis, because of the contribution of the treatment variance to the weights. This is illustrated in the guide, where we demonstrate how decreasing the amount of time observed before the policy change shifts the two-way fixed effects estimate but not the other estimates. The guide demonstrates this bias; it uses the Goodman Bacon decomposition to show that the two-way fixed effects estimate is influenced by comparisons between earlier and later treated units that no epidemiologist would actually want to make.
